1:
The book opens by naming a man and a place, and the witnesses find both charged with meaning. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great fastens on the geography as praise: we are told where the holy man dwelt because Uz was a land of the Gentiles, and it is no great thing to be good in the company of the good, but immeasurably high testimony to have shown oneself good among the wicked. As Peter commended just Lot, whose righteous soul was vexed from day to day by the deeds he saw and heard, so Job was a brother to dragons and a companion to owls, and yet upright; and their evil lives struck his eyes and ears not with pleasure but with the pain of a blow.

The reformed John Gill and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott labour over the location. Gill traces the land of Uz not to the descendant of Shem but to Uz the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, or possibly to Uz of the children of Seir in Edom, and settles it in one of the Arabias — Deserta rather than Petraea — near the Sabeans, the Chaldeans, and the land of Edom. Ellicott counts three men named Uz in Genesis — a son of Aram, the firstborn of Nahor, and a son of Seir the Horite — and, weighing the mention of the land of Uz beside Edom in Lam. 4:21 and Jer. 25:20, places Job's home in the district south and southeast of Palestine. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following Mr. Good, is more emphatic still: all the persons of the poem are Edomite Arabs of Idumea, so that the land of Uz and the land of Edom are convertible terms; John Wesley says simply, part of Arabia.

On the man's character the voices converge. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds a fourfold portrait — Job feared God, was perfect (not sinless, for he owns in Job 9:20 that if he called himself perfect he would be proved perverse, but sincere), upright in all his dealings, and one who eschewed evil out of the fear of God — and marvels that he was eminently good in so bad a place. Ellicott sets the same word "perfect" beside Noah in Gen. 6:9 and the standard Christ required of his disciples in Matt. 5:48, finding here the very wisdom of Job 28:28. Wesley glosses "perfect" as sincere intention, not legal exactness.

Beneath the agreement runs a quiet dispute about the book itself. Clarke, having weighed the endless questions Calmet raised, believes Job a real person whose history is fact, but argues from the book's frequent echoes of the Mosaic institutions that he lived after the giving of the Law, and that Moses, during his years in Midian, most likely wrote it. Against this stands the older view, that Job lived in the patriarchal age soon after — or even before — Abraham, near the Ur from which Abraham was called, and that the book is the most ancient in existence, likely written by Job himself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lift the eye above these puzzles to the question the whole book exists to answer: why do afflictions upon afflictions befall the righteous man?
2:
A single line records the birth of Job's children, and the witnesses read the bare census as an emblem of his blessedness. The reformed John Gill notes only that these seven sons and three daughters were born to him by his wife, in lawful wedlock — she who was still living and would appear again later in the story. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes more of the count: some of each sex, and more of the more noble sex in which a family is built up. Children are to be looked upon as blessings, a heritage of the Lord and his reward, as Ps. 127:3 has it, especially to good people who will give them good instruction, set them good examples, and put up good prayers for them. It was an instance of Job's prosperity, Henry says, that his house was filled with children, and yet he was neither oppressive nor uncharitable but liberal to the poor.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch step back to survey the whole estate the verse begins to enumerate. It is a large, princely household; the numbers are large, but must not on that account be reckoned an invention. They observe how the narrative chooses its verbs — forms that signify not merely being but coming-to-be — to plant the reader at once in the midst of Job's flourishing, and they quote Leo Africanus that the Arabs measure their very wealth and possessions by their flocks, so that to number Job's animals is to take the measure of his greatness. Among the sons of the east, they add, Job was without an equal.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, looks past the beginning of the book to its end and catches a deliberate symmetry: the like number of seven sons and three daughters was restored to Job after his probation, as Job 42:13 records. The detail is not idle; it belongs to the architecture of the whole, the first estate answered exactly by the last.

The witnesses do not divide. Together they let the small statistic carry its weight: that Job's happiness was complete in the ordinary and precious goods of family, that these were God's gift and not his own achievement, and that the very fulness here set down — ten children, gathered and beloved — is recorded so early precisely because it is all to be swept away. The reader who is told, at the very outset, how richly Job was blessed in his sons and daughters is being prepared, though he does not yet know it, to feel the whole weight of their loss. What the verse offers as a picture of settled happiness the story will shortly turn into the measure of a father's grief; and the witnesses, by lingering over the blessing, teach us to reckon the cost of the trial to come.
3:
The inventory of Job's wealth — seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred she-asses, and a very great household — draws the witnesses to count, to explain, and to weigh what such greatness meant. The reformed John Gill observes that the sheep are named first because they were the largest and most useful part, yielding wool for clothing and flesh for food, requiring a large pasturage to feed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reflects that riches are here called "substance" after the common way of speaking, though to the soul they are but shadows, things that are not, as Prov. 23:5 warns; Job's estate is reckoned not by acres but by cattle and servants, for in those early days a man might have land enough if he had but wherewithal to stock it, and dominion over the creatures was ever a chief instance of wealth and honour, as Ps. 8:6 declares.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses supply the particulars. Adam Clarke reports how the Targum divides the substance — a thousand sheep for each son, a thousand camels for each daughter, five hundred yoke of oxen for Job himself, and five hundred she-asses for his wife — and glosses the "very great household" as a very great estate of husbandry, embracing every sort of field-labour and servant; Job, he says, was the chief emir of that district, eminent above all in wisdom, wealth, and piety. John Wesley adds that camels in those parts were numerous and useful, able to endure thirst and to serve in war, and that the she-asses are named because they were the most valued.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott close the reckoning. Keil and Delitzsch confirm that this made Job the greatest of all the sons of the east, the tribes stretching from Arabia Deserta northward; the enumeration is no idle boast but the very substance of his rank. Ellicott notes that the phrase "the men of the east" is indefinite and might embrace all the neighbouring districts, and remarks that the Arabs still call the region east of Jordan the land of Job — a lovely and fertile country, fulfilling the conditions of the poem.

The voices do not contend. Together they render Job not merely rich but the greatest of a whole region, his flocks and herds the visible token of a prosperity that his piety had not forfeited but, if anything, increased. Henry's earlier verdict hangs over the scene — that Job was upright and honest, and yet grew rich, nay, therefore grew rich, for the account of his substance is set down before the history of his afflictions to show that neither wealth nor godliness can secure a man from the calamities that are coming.
4:
The narrative turns to a gentler scene — the grown sons feasting in their houses, each on his day, and sending for their three sisters — and the witnesses read in it a picture of a family both prosperous and at peace. The reformed John Gill infers that the sons were come to man's estate, settled in houses of their own and carrying separate business, who met by turns not for intemperance or wantonness (which Job would never have countenanced) but to cherish love and maintain harmony among themselves; the feasts, he suggests, may have fallen at sheep-shearing or some like season, kept in their own homes and not in public houses.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells tenderly on the comfort such a scene gave the father. It was Job's joy to see his children grown and settled, thriving enough to feast one another, in health, and above all living in love and unity, with no jars or quarrels but as much freedom as if they had had all in common. He notes the brothers' kindness in sending for their modest sisters, who would not have gone unbidden, and the decency of a feast fit for such company. Job himself did not join them — not from sourness, but, like Barzillai in 2 Sam. 19:35, he was old and dead to these things and would let the young be free; yet he did not deny them the youthful liberty he denied himself, provided they fled youthful lusts.

Over one small phrase the witnesses gently divide. "Every one his day" the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes to mean a birthday festival, each brother in turn inviting the rest when his own came round; the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees it was probably his birthday, comparing the birthday feasts of Gen. 40:20 and of Herod in Mark 6:21. John Wesley allows the birthday but also offers the first day of the month; while Gill, less sure it was a nativity, reads it rather as an appointed day in a settled rotation. Whether birthday or fixed turn, all agree the feasts were innocent, held to testify and maintain brotherly love.

The scene is thus one of unclouded domestic happiness, and the witnesses let it stand as such — the more affecting because the reader already knows, from the council in heaven, that this bright and loving circle is precisely the mark at which the accuser is taking aim. The very unity and gladness that Job rejoiced to see are being set before us so that their sudden ruin, when the great wind comes, may fall with its full weight.
5:
When the round of feasting had gone about, Job would send and sanctify his children, rise early, and offer a burnt-offering for each, saying, "It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts" — and the witnesses gather round this portrait of a father's priestly care. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as a godly jealousy: Job feared that in their mirth his children might have been too merry, taken too great a liberty, and entertained atheistical or profane thoughts, so that when the feasting was over their good father called them to solemn ordinances, sanctified them, rose early as one whose heart was on his work, and offered a sacrifice for every child, that they might be humbled for sin and led to a Mediator. Thus he did continually, for, as John 13:10 teaches, he that is washed still needs to wash his feet.

The reformed John Gill and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the custom. Gill takes it of the end of each rotation; Keil and Delitzsch note how the verbs describe an action repeated habitually in the past, the settled practice of a devout man. Charles Ellicott seizes on the father acting as priest for his household — one of the marks that Job stood outside the pale of the Mosaic law, his life answering rather to the patriarchs of Genesis.

Over the phrase "cursed God" the witnesses openly differ, for the Hebrew word is really "blessed." Gill, Henry, and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keep the plain sense — Wesley glossing it not as gross cursing (which Job would hardly suspect) but as despising or slighting God, giving him no praise for mercies enjoyed. Ellicott reads the word as literally "bless," a euphemism, or perhaps a bidding-farewell to and so dismissing of God. Adam Clarke, most adventurous, weighs whether Job feared his children had "blessed the gods" in some idolatrous thought, or, with Mr. Good, renders it "nor blessed God in their hearts," though he owns the received sense is the plainer.

Beneath the philology the witnesses are one on the man. Whether the dreaded sin was a curse, a cold dismissal, or a lapse into idolatry, Job's response is the same: he will not presume upon his children's piety but covers even their unknown and secret faults with sacrifice, rising early and doing it continually. Ellicott and Wesley alike draw the lesson that parents should be particular in their addresses to God for each branch of the family, praying for every child according to his own temper and need — a portrait of anxious, unwearied love that the coming verses will make unbearably poignant.
6:
The scene shifts abruptly from earth to the unseen world, where the sons of God come to present themselves before the LORD and Satan comes also among them — and the witnesses meet the strange council on several fronts at once. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great sets it in a wide frame: Holy Writ is a mirror in which we see our inward face, and it shows us not only the excellencies of the saints but their mischances, so that Job is described as made greater by temptation while David was by temptation brought to the ground — that the virtue of our forerunners may cherish hope and their falls brace us to humility.

Who, then, are these "sons of God"? The reformed John Gill takes them for the angels, so called by reason of their creation, their likeness to God in holiness and knowledge, and their obedience, who stand before him and go forth to do his will. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees they probably mean the angels, or at least an incident in the unseen world running parallel to worship on earth. But the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry allows a second reading — that this may be a meeting of the saints on earth, professors of religion who in the patriarchal age were called sons of God, as in Gen. 6:2 — among whom Satan thrust himself as a serpent into paradise; though he also expounds it, with the others, as an assembly of angels into which the fallen Lucifer intrudes, summoned as a criminal or connived at for the time.

A second question divides them: is the scene literal or figurative? Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley read it as parabolical, like Micaiah's vision in 1 Kings 22:19 — an allegory teaching that God governs all the actions of men and devils, and that the affairs of earth are the subject of the counsels of an unseen world that lies open to us. Adam Clarke, with Mr. Peters, calls it rather the prophetic way of representing a real transaction: as kings hold council, so God is pleased to show himself passing the decrees of his providence in an assembly of his holy ones, a representation founded upon the settled truth of good and bad angels.

Clarke presses that truth into a warning of his own. The word is hassatan, the adversary, whom Peter names our adversary the devil in 1 Pet. 5:8; and it is now fashionable, he complains, to deny this evil spirit's existence — one of the very depths of Satan, since those who deny his being will not watch or pray against him, and so become his easy and unopposing prey. The witnesses converge on the marvel Henry names: a Satan among the sons of God, an intruder in the holy assembly, whose access to the presence of God is nonetheless under God's own check and control.
7:
God opens the interview with a question — "Whence comest thou?" — and the witnesses agree at once that it is put not for God's information but for Satan's exposure. The reformed John Gill insists the omniscient God knows every person and place, and asks either in resentment at the intruder, chiding him as having no business there, or, more likely, to draw out from him what he had marked in his roamings, and so to lead on to the mention of Job. How God and spirits converse we cannot say, but there is a way in which he speaks with them, good and evil alike, and this does not touch the reality of the narrative.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar and the character it reveals. The form of the verb gives the present, "whence comest thou," and Cocceius subtly observes that Satan is noted as one acting as if unapproved of God, his business selfish and arbitrary, with no connection to God's work. His answer, "from going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it," they parse closely — one word for a rapid passing from end to end, the other for an observant roaming; and they hear Peter's echo, who says the adversary walks about, whence indeed our word "peripatetic," while the Arabs call the devil el-hharith, the busy, industrious one. He answers only in general, they add, as expecting the more particular question God is about to put.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the same restless motion. He surveys the old versions — the Septuagint's "having gone round the earth and walked over all under heaven," the Chaldee's "to examine the works of the children of men" — and, with Coverdale, inclines to take the word for "earth" as "that land" rather than the whole globe. The verb, he notes, stands in the intensive conjugation, showing how earnest and determined the devil is: he sets himself to walk, is busily employed, seeking men's destruction, and while they sleep he wakes, so that the country folk, seeing a man bent on mischief, say plainly, "The devil is busy with him." Charles Ellicott adds only that Peter clearly had this passage in mind when he wrote that the adversary walketh about, as 1 Pet. 5:8 declares.

The witnesses do not divide. They leave us an accuser summoned to give account of his wanderings — evasive, general, restless, unable to plead any good and unwilling to own any harm — and a God who keeps the initiative wholly in his own hand, drawing the enemy out before ever a word of accusation can be spoken.
8:
God himself names the man the accuser has come to attack — "Hast thou considered my servant Job? there is none like him in the earth" — and the witnesses hear in the question both a challenge to Satan and an honour to Job. The reformed John Gill renders the Hebrew "hast thou set thy heart upon my servant Job," and reads it as more than a casual notice: Satan had indeed fixed his heart upon Job, not in love but in longing to have him in his hands, as he desired to have Peter; the question is at once a sarcasm and an expression of God's indignation, as if to say, thou hast contrived how to attack and draw him from my service, but all in vain.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the little word "for" gives the ground of the inquiry: had Satan truly observed Job, even he must have confessed that genuine piety exists on the earth. They mark it a skilful touch of the poet that the four predicates first used of Job — perfect, upright, one that feareth God, that escheweth evil — are now taken up again in the mouth of the LORD himself, the divine testimony repeating the narrator's. Adam Clarke reads the phrase the same way: hast thou placed thy heart on my servant Job, viewed his conduct with attention, while thou wast roaming about seeking whom thou mightest devour?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the tenderness and the strategy of it. God speaks honourably of Job — "he is my servant" — for good men are God's servants, whom he counts himself honoured to own; and "none like him," none valued like him among all the potentates of earth, though those in heaven far outshine him. Henry finds a threefold design in the LORD's giving Satan this good character: to aggravate the apostasy of the wicked spirit by so unlike a pattern; to answer the devil's boast of dominion over the earth with "Job is my faithful servant"; and to anticipate his accusation before it is uttered — "Satan, I know thy errand; thou art come to inform against Job, but does not his unquestionable character give thee the lie?" So God knows all the malice of the enemy against his servants, and we have an advocate ready to appear for us before ever we are accused.

The witnesses stand together. They make the verse the pivot on which the whole trial turns: God does not wait to be told of Job but himself names him, glories in him, and flings his integrity in the accuser's face — the divine boast that both invites the assault and, unknown to Satan, guarantees that the servant so commended will be upheld.
9:
The accuser cannot deny Job's goodness, so he impeaches its motive: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" The reformed John Gill observes how much the question concedes — Satan charges Job with no single sin, does not even deny that he fears God, but insinuates by a sly query that his religion is not "for nought," not free, but mercenary, kept up for worldly gain; and this cowardly way of slander, suggesting by a question what one dares not assert, many of the devil's children have learned from him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the accusation in its cosmic setting. Satan is the accuser who, as Rev. 12:10 says, accuses the servants of God day and night; so long as he is not finally condemned he has access to God, and thinks to justify himself by denying that any true and lasting piety can exist. God permits it, for evil in the world of spirits is left free to maintain and expand itself until a stronger power comes against it. Charles Ellicott names this the worst kind of scepticism — a disbelief in human goodness itself; Satan knows that the motive is an action's only value, and so calumniates Job's motives. Here, Ellicott says, the object of the whole book is introduced: to exhibit the integrity of human conduct under the worst possible trial, and to show a man victorious over Satan.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the charge and its half-truth. It was true, he grants, that Job did not fear God for nought, for godliness is great gain; but it was a lie that he would not have feared God without it. The devil could endure to hear no one praised, not even by God; unable to accuse Job of any evil, he charged him with by-ends in doing good — for it is easy for those who seek an occasion to brand the blameless with hypocrisy. Yet Henry draws the needful distinction: it is not mercenary to look to the eternal recompense in our obedience, but to aim at temporal advantage and make religion serve it is a spiritual idolatry, worshipping the creature above the Creator, since men cannot long serve God and mammon.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the accuser, beaten from every honest charge, retreats to the one accusation that can never quite be disproved by argument but only by trial — that goodness is a bargain — and that God, by permitting the wager, undertakes to answer the slander not with words but with the spectacle of a man who will fear him for nothing.
10:
Satan grounds his charge in the very favour that surrounds Job — "Hast not thou made an hedge about him?" — and the witnesses read the accusation as a grudging confession of God's care. The reformed John Gill dwells on the hedge as a wall of protection thrown about Job on every side: God's love as a shield, his power, his providence, his encamping angels, his own presence as a wall of fire, so thick a fence that Satan could not find the least gap to enter and do him harm; and it was this very hedge that the wicked one, vexed, maliciously turned into the sole reason for Job's piety.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the image: God had fortified Job as with spikes and spears, an unapproachable hedge, so that he was the object of a peculiar care and not exposed to the common trials of life. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry rounds out the double picture the verse gives. God had both protected Job — a hedge about his person, family, and possessions, for his peculiar people are taken under special protection — and prospered him, blessing the work of his hands; for without that blessing the strongest and most skilful hands cannot make the work prosper, but with it Job's substance wonderfully increased. The blessing of the LORD makes rich, Henry notes, and Satan himself here owns it. Yet the devil speaks of it all with vexation, as one who had walked round the hedge seeking a single gap and found none, and argued that Job served God only because God paid him so well.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lift the matter to a graver level. The permission God is about to give, they observe, appears at the same time as a divine command, for God is never merely passive; he is even called in Scripture the creator of calamity — the evil act alone excepted — as Isa. 45:7 declares. And they are careful that the coming affliction has no foundation in any sin clinging to Job, since the very praise conferred on him rules that out.

The witnesses hold together. They let Satan's sneer become, against his will, a testimony: that Job was indeed hedged and blessed by a God who owns him, and that the accuser's only quarrel is with grace itself — as though a man could not truly love the God who has been good to him. The whole wager turns on whether that hedge, once lowered, will leave a piety that grace had merely purchased, or a piety that grace had truly made.
11:
Now the accuser lays down his wager — "But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face." The reformed John Gill weighs each word. Satan asks God to withdraw the hand of providence that had covered Job and to stretch out instead a hand of wrath, consuming all he had; and he wants it done "now," at once, in the midst of Job's prosperity, for the enemy is ever in haste to do mischief. The Vulgate's "touch him a little," Gill notes, misses the mark, for Satan knew Job's integrity too well to think a slight trial would betray it — which is why he immediately raises the stakes to "all that he hath."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the challenge as a cynic's creed. "Shoot the dart of poverty and affliction against him," and Job "will bless thee only to thy appearances" — will be pious only in proportion to the temporal good thou bestowest; if thou art gracious, he will be devout. It is the exact maxim of the statesman who held that every man has his price. But Clarke turns the sneer back: God has multitudes who will not sell their souls or consciences at any price, who, though he slay them, will yet trust in him — so did Job, so have thousands, so will all in whose hearts Christ dwells by faith.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks how slightly, and how spitefully, the devil speaks — as if a little cross would change Job's tone, and as if he would not merely fall from his devotion but turn it into open defiance and "curse thee to thy face." Henry notes that the word rendered "curse" is really the word for "bless," for cursing God is so impious a thing that the holy tongue would not name it plainly, though the sense here is clearly a curse, as in the charge against Naboth in 1 Kings 21:10. And he unfolds the vast stake: if Job, impoverished, would renounce his religion, Satan would have made out his own universal empire over mankind and proved that God had not one faithful servant, that piety itself was a sham; but it appeared that the LORD knows them that are his and is deceived in none.

The witnesses do not divide. They set before us the whole gamble of the book — the accuser certain that a lowered hedge will expose a hireling's heart, God willing to let the trial go forward — and leave the issue hanging on the single question whether Job's fear of God can outlast the loss of everything God had given him.
12:
God grants the trial, but with a leash upon it — "Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand" — and the witnesses dwell on both the astonishing grant and its strict limit. The reformed John Gill is careful to read the permission rightly: God gave it not because he was displeased with Job, nor to gratify Satan, but to convince and confound the accuser and to try the grace of his servant, that it might shine the brighter. And he insists that the LORD alone had the sovereign disposal of all Job's estate; Satan could have no power over him or his but what was expressly given him.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the comfort of that bound. Adam Clarke observes that Satan cannot deprive a man even of an ass or a sheep or a pig but by God's special permission — his power and malice are ever bounded and under control — and notes the Targum's addition that Satan went forth "with authority from the presence of the LORD." John Wesley owns it seems strange that God should give such a permission at all, yet he did it for his own glory, for the honour of Job, for the explanation of providence, and for the encouragement of his afflicted people in every age.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the same point the settled teaching of Scripture: mighty as the principle of evil is in the world, it is held in check by One who directs it to his own ends, so that we are not under the uncontrolled dominion of evil, strong as the temptation is at times to think so, as 2 Cor. 12:7 reminds us. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the wonder and the comfort together: it is matter of wonder that God should deliver the soul of his turtle-dove into the hand of the adversary, such a lamb to such a lion — yet he did it to make of Job's case a useful precedent for all his suffering people, as he suffered Peter to be sifted but took care his faith should not fail, in Luke 22:31. And it is matter of comfort that God has the devil in a chain, in a great chain, as Rev. 20:1 shows; Satan could not touch Job without leave, and then no further than his leave allowed — his body reserved, only his estate exposed.

With that the accuser departs, and the witnesses note him going forth glad that he had gained his point and resolved to lose no time, no longer wandering to and fro but making straight for the man who, all unknowing, goes quietly on in the way of his duty.
13:
The trial begins on a chosen day — while Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house — and the witnesses attend to the sinister timing of it. The reformed John Gill cannot fix the exact day, and doubts it was the very morrow of Satan's leave, since it took time to bring the Sabeans and Chaldeans marching out of their own countries into Job's; the enemy, though eager and in haste, would contrive and fix upon the fittest hour to answer his ends.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add a poignant detail from the narrative's own order: it was on the very day when Job had celebrated the usual morning worship with his children and knew them gathered at the eldest son's house, the round of mutual entertainment come again to its beginning, that the messengers of misfortune broke in upon him. The blow falls, that is, at the moment of the family's fullest joy and the father's freshest devotion.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes this deliberate cruelty the heart of the verse. Satan brought the troubles on the very day the children began their course of feasting at the eldest brother's, where, having the double portion, the entertainment was richest and the whole family at perfect repose, under no apprehension of trouble; and this time the enemy chose that the calamity, coming then, might be the more grievous — the night of their pleasure turned into fear, as Isa. 21:4 laments. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the Targum's tradition that it was the first day of the week, and takes it for one of those birthday festivals already mentioned.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they let the timing preach. It was no accident that ruin came at the hour of feasting; the accuser, granted his hour, waited for the moment when Job had most to lose and least expected loss, so that the stroke might land with its whole weight. Keil and Delitzsch's quiet note — that Job had that very morning worshipped and sanctified his children — sets the scene in its full pathos: a father's piety and a family's gladness are the very things the enemy has marked, and the reader, who has watched the council in heaven, knows that the peace of the eldest brother's house is about to be shattered from a quarter none of them can see. The stage is set for the four blows that follow, each treading upon the heels of the last.
14:
The first messenger arrives, breathless — "The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them" — and the witnesses begin to trace the pattern of the assault. The reformed John Gill pauses to correct an old fancy: this messenger was no evil spirit or angel of Satan, as some Rabbins and even some ancient Christian writers supposed, but simply one of Job's own servants who had escaped the calamity that swept away his fellows.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the scene of ordinary industry the disaster interrupts — the oxen at the plough, the she-asses grazing quietly beside them — the very picture of a well-ordered estate going peacefully about its work when ruin falls. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, adds only the small realistic touch that the she-asses are named because they were the more domesticated and valued, kept for their milk and their labour.

The other wesleyan-arminian witness, John Wesley, fastens on the relentless design behind the messengers. One followed immediately upon another, Satan so ordering it, by God's permission, that there might seem to be more than ordinary displeasure of God against Job in his troubles, and that the sufferer might have no leisure to recollect himself but be overwhelmed by a complication of calamities at once. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the report the same way and draws out its mercies and its terrors together. The loss was not through any carelessness of the servants — the oxen were ploughing, not straying, each in its place under the servant's eye — so that all our prudence and diligence cannot secure us from affliction; yet it is some comfort under trouble if it finds us in the way of our duty. And the single survivor was spared, Henry says, not in kindness but that Job might have certain intelligence of the blow by an eye-witness, before a slower rumour could break it to him gradually.

The witnesses converge on the artfulness of the stroke. The messenger's very words — that the beasts were about their honest work when the blow fell — leave Job no one to blame, no negligence on which his resentment might spend itself; and the drumbeat refrain, "I only am escaped alone to tell thee," which will toll four times over, is heard here for the first time. The trial is contrived, they agree, not merely to strip Job of his goods but to crowd the losses so close together that grief can find no breathing-space, and to leave him, at each turn, with nothing but the bare hand of God to look to.
15:
The blow itself is named — "The Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants" — and the witnesses turn to identify the raiders. The reformed John Gill reads the Hebrew as "Sheba fell," a host or company of Sabeans, and traces them not to the Sheba descended from Ham or Shem but to Sheba the son of Jokshan, Abraham's son by Keturah, whose posterity were sent into the east country and became Job's near neighbours. They dwelt, he argues, not in the plentiful Arabia Felix — too rich to need to plunder, and too far off, lying to the south — but in the barren Arabia Deserta, whence Scripture speaks of Sabeans from the wilderness.

The witnesses part, mildly, over the very word. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes that the Vulgate alone takes "Sheba" for a settled people, while the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic understand a marauding party, and the Chaldee turns it into a legend, that Lilith, queen of Zamargad, rushed suddenly upon them. Clarke himself reconciles the readings: these were hordes of predatory banditti, descended indeed from Abraham by Keturah, who inhabited Arabia Deserta east of Uz and made sudden incursions, carrying off men, cattle, and goods and retiring into the desert where none could pursue — a manner of life, he adds, that continues in those countries to the present day. John Wesley agrees they were a people of Arabia who led a wandering life and lived by robbery and spoil.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the three men named Sheba in Genesis — the grandson of Cush, the grandson of Abraham through Jokshan, and the grandson of Eber — and judges it probably the second who is meant, whose descendants led a predatory and marauding life in the country bordering on Job's, as Ezek. 38:13 may suggest.

Whether "the Sabeans" names a settled tribe or a roving band, the witnesses agree on the substance: a real people of the near desert, kin to Abraham, fell suddenly on Job's ploughing oxen and grazing asses, killed the herdsmen, and drove off the beasts. And each closes on the same tolling refrain, "I only am escaped alone to tell thee" — the survivor spared, as Wesley says, precisely that Job might have speedy and certain word of his calamity. The first stroke has fallen; before its messenger can finish, another is already at the door.
16:
Before the first messenger has done, a second breaks in with a stranger horror — "The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants." The reformed John Gill marks the merciless speed of it: this man came before the former had finished his account, Satan so ordering that the afflictions should fall thick and fast, allowing Job no breathing-time, no space for prayer to support him or for meditation on past mercies, but hurrying one blow upon another to startle him into some rash word against God.

On the nature of the fire the witnesses are of one mind. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it for lightning — as thunder was reckoned the voice of God, so lightning was his fire — and supposes the prince of the power of the air, now armed with this artillery of heaven, directed the zigzag flame across the fields to destroy the whole flock in a moment. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees it can hardly mean anything but lightning, comparing the fire of Gen. 19:24 and of 2 Kings 1:10; it is the way of Old Testament poetry to see in the convulsions of nature the immediate action of the Most High, though here, he thinks, we are meant to see more, since the book assumes to record a divine revelation. John Wesley reads it the same way and hears its cruel suggestion — the tidings came, as it were, immediately from the hand of God, and seemed to show that God was angry at Job's very offerings and would receive no more from his hands.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds that suggestion as Satan's real design. The sheep, the very beasts with which Job had honoured God in sacrifice, were taken as if God would punish him in the things he had used in his service; having misrepresented Job to God as a false servant, the accuser now misrepresents God to Job as a hard Master who would not protect the flocks from which so many burnt-offerings came, tempting him to think it vain to serve God. Had fire from heaven consumed the sheep upon the altar, Job might have read it as a token of favour; consuming them in the pasture, he could scarcely but feel it a token of displeasure — a destruction from God, which Job elsewhere owned was a terror to him.

The witnesses do not divide. They see one lightning-stroke doing double work: it destroyed the flock, and it whispered to the stricken man that heaven itself had turned against him — the subtlest cruelty of all, that the God he served should seem to have become his enemy.
17:
The third messenger comes on the heels of the second — "The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels" — and the witnesses turn to these new raiders from the opposite quarter. The reformed John Gill notes only that this servant, too, arrived before the last had finished. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the history: the Chaldeans dwelt on both sides of the Euphrates near Babylon, mixed with the wandering Arabs and living like them on rapine; they were the descendants of Chesed, son of Nahor and brother of Huz, from whom came their name Casdim, and they divided into three bands the more effectually to surround and drive off the three thousand camels.

The grammatical-historical witnesses add the philology and a chronological quarrel. Charles Ellicott derives them from Chesed in Gen. 22:22, tracing the name through Carduchia and Kurdistan as well as Chaldaea, and observes that this calamity arose from the opposite quarter to the last — an apt illustration that troubles never come alone, and that causes of the most different kinds seem to combine against a falling man. Keil and Delitzsch, however, must defend the passage against those who would use it to date the book late. Ewald, they report, sees in the very mention of the Chaldeans a mark of composition in the seventh century, when the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar rose to power, and Renan holds that they first appear as such marauders about the time of Uzziah; but Keil and Delitzsch answer that Genesis already knows early Semitic Chaldeans among the mountains north of Assyria, and Nahor-Chaldeans of Mesopotamia whose existence reaches back to patriarchal times, so that their raid on Job proves nothing of a late date.

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, adds simply that the Chaldeans lived upon spoil, as Xenophon and others observe.

The witnesses converge on the meaning of the twofold assault. Sabeans from the south had taken the oxen and asses; now Chaldeans from the north sweep off the camels — the two robber-nations closing on Job from opposite directions, as if the whole earth had risen against him. And the same refrain tolls a third time, "I only am escaped alone to tell thee." Beneath the scholars' dispute over dates lies a shared certainty: these were real marauding peoples, kin in their lawless life, and their coming from north and south alike leaves Job, in a single hour, stripped of the last of his herds and braced, though he cannot know it, for a heavier blow than any yet.
18:
The fourth messenger enters while the third is still speaking, and his opening words fall like a knell — "Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house." The reformed John Gill notes simply that this was a servant who had been in attendance at the feast, the scene already set before us now returning with dreadful purpose.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording that carries the horror. The small change of particle — "while" in place of the "yet" of the earlier reports — marks a continuity in space rather than time, the messengers treading one upon another; the word for the young people is that epicene term of the Pentateuch which embraces both the sons and the daughters together; and the wind that is coming, they observe, sweeps "from the other side of the desert," that is, from its farthest end. In one day, they sum up, Job is now to be bereft of everything he had accounted the gift of Jehovah.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, lifts the eye from the detail to the design. This marvellous accumulation of disasters — four crushing blows in a single afternoon, each announced by a sole survivor, and now the refrain "I only am escaped alone to tell thee" tolling for the fourth and last time — points us, he says, to the conclusion that it was the distinct work of Satan, according to the permission granted him earlier in v.12, and therefore, in its very concentration, no ordinary run of misfortune but supernatural.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brevity of their comment here is itself eloquent, for the verse is only the doorway to the worst. The messenger names, deliberately and without haste, the peaceful and happy scene the reader remembers — the ten children gathered in love at the eldest brother's table, the very picture of v.4 — before he shatters it in the next breath. Satan has kept his heaviest stroke for the last, and the narrative, by pausing to recall the feast in its innocence, makes the reader feel the whole weight of what is about to fall. The oxen, the sheep, the camels were but the outworks; now the enemy comes at the citadel of Job's heart, his children, and the sentence that began so gently is poised to end in the ruin of them all. What the earlier reports could take from Job was only his substance; this last one aims at his very affections, and the witnesses let its slow, familiar opening deepen the dread of the blow to come.
19:
The last messenger completes his errand — "there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead" — and the witnesses stand before the ruin of Job's whole family. The reformed John Gill notes the wind came most likely from the wilderness of Arabia, whence such blasts are strong; it was so violent and so extraordinary in its effect that a "behold" is set before it to rouse the reader's wonder. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, sees here another proof of the prince of the power of the air: he directed four several currents against the four corners or sides of the house at once, crushing it together and burying all within in one common ruin.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the turning-point in Job's own bearing. The first three messengers he had heard sitting and in silence; but at the news of his children's death he can no longer overcome his grief, and rises — not, however, as one in despair, but humbling himself under the mighty hand of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the other wesleyan-arminian witness, John Wesley, dwell on why this loss was kept for the last. It was the greatest of Job's losses, they agree, and Satan reserved it that, if the other provocations failed, this might make him curse God. The children died together and suddenly, Henry observes, and — bitterest of all to their praying father — they died feasting rather than praying, taken unawares like a thief in the night, and now beyond the reach of the sacrifices he had daily offered on their behalf. They died, both note, by a wind of the devil's raising, the prince of the power of the air, as Eph. 2:2 names him; yet it looked like the immediate hand of God, and so Bildad would afterward construe it in Job 8:4, that the children had sinned and God had cast them away. And they were taken, Wesley adds, just when Job had most need of them to comfort him under his other losses — such miserable comforters are all creatures, and in God alone have we a constant and sufficient help.

The witnesses converge on the sheer magnitude of the blow. In a single day Job has lost his servants, his oxen and asses, his sheep, his camels, and now all ten of his children at once — the accuser's masterstroke, a devil's wind that wore the mask of God's own displeasure. Everything Jehovah had given is gone; only the man himself remains, and the question of the whole trial now hangs upon what he will do.
20:
Now the narrative fixes on the man himself — "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped" — and the witnesses watch closely to see whether the accuser's prophecy will come true. The reformed John Gill lingers on the word "then": through the loss of his substance Job had sat and heard sedately, without stopping the messengers, but at the tidings of his children's death he arose, deeply moved, yet with strength of body and vigour of mind still unbroken, going about what followed with great composure.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole conduct as that of a man both feeling and faithful. Job did not behave like a stock or a stone, unnatural and unaffected at the death of his children; he arose as a champion to the combat, and rent his mantle and shaved his head, the usual tokens of great sorrow, showing that he was sensible of the hand of God gone out against him — yet he broke into no indecent passion, kept his temper, and maintained the possession of his own soul. Then, like a wise and good man, he humbled himself under God's hand, falling to the ground in penitent submission and accepting the punishment; for hypocrites, Henry notes from Job 36:13, cry not when God binds them. He adds the guess of some, that Job rent his clothes in holy indignation at the blasphemous thoughts Satan was casting into his mind.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the gestures as ancient signs of grief bent toward God. Adam Clarke lists the tearing of garments, the shaving of the head, the dust upon it, the sitting on the ground, as acts by which immoderate grief was expressed, and insists Job felt the bitterness keenly, as any true man must; "worshipped," he says, means Job prostrated himself, his face in the dust. John Wesley marks the same shaving as a customary mourning rite, and fastens on the wonder of the last word: instead of cursing God, as Satan had foretold, Job adored him, and gave him the glory of his sovereignty, his justice, and his goodness in this most severe dispensation.

Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, sets Job's act beside David's in 2 Sam. 12:20 and Hezekiah's in 2 Kings 19:1, observing that moments of intense sorrow, like moments of intense joy, force us into the immediate presence of God; and Keil and Delitzsch confirm that Job, for all the intensity of his feeling, acts not as one in despair but as one humbling himself under the mighty hand. The witnesses do not divide: at the very point where the accuser looked for a curse, Job falls down and worships.
21:
Job's words rise out of the dust — "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" — and the witnesses gather round the confession that answers the whole wager. The reformed John Gill takes the nakedness literally, of the body at birth and at death: not the soul's nakedness of righteousness, which would ill suit the blessing that follows, but the plain truth that we bring nothing into the world, as Paul urges in 1 Tim. 6:7, a text he thinks may look back to this very saying.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the quieting considerations by which Job composed himself. Reasoning from the common state of human life, Job saw that he was but where he was at first — naked, not maimed, still his own man when nothing else was his own — and but where he must be at last, unclothed a little sooner than he expected, as one who puts off his clothes near bed-time. Above all, Job looked past the instruments to the first Cause: he did not say "the Sabeans and Chaldeans have taken away," but "the LORD hath taken," and for that reason held his peace, owning God's hand in his comforts once given and in his crosses now sent, and adoring the very name of God even in the taking away.

Over one word the witnesses divide. "Naked shall I return thither" — thither where? The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke denies it means the mother's womb, and takes "there" to point to the ground on which Job was that moment falling, to which he would return as he had come. But John Wesley, with Ellicott and Henry, reads it of the womb understood as our common mother the earth, into whose lap we lay our heads as a weary child, an echo of the sentence of Gen. 3:19. Clarke also records the Chaldee's reverent expansion, "the Word of the LORD gave, and the Word of the LORD hath taken away."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott seals the scene with a single stroke: "Blessed be the name of the LORD" is the very word Satan had used in a contrary sense in v.11, when he foretold that Job would "curse" God to his face — so that with this blessing Satan was, for the first time, utterly foiled. The witnesses do not divide on the heart of it: stripped of everything, Job neither accuses the raiders nor arraigns his God, but traces both gift and loss to one hand and blesses the name that gave and took.
22:
The prologue's first act closes with the narrator's verdict — "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly" — and the witnesses weigh both the vindication and its careful terms. The reformed John Gill is precise: it does not mean Job was sinless, for he was conscious of sin and owns it elsewhere, but that in all he did and said under this stroke — the rending, the shaving, the prostration, the words from his lips — there was nothing unbecoming a religious man, and above all nothing of the sin Satan had foretold, that he would curse God to his face; of that there was not a trace, but the very reverse.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes this the transaction that gave the vivid colouring to Job's whole character: here, and here alone, he was the very pattern of patience and resignation, satisfied under the privation as he had been under the affluence, charging God with no unkindness; and in this Satan was utterly disappointed, having reckoned Job would barter his God for his goods as so many others had done. Clarke adds, from this same steadiness in worship, a note toward the older debate about the book's date — that Job's continual burnt-offerings answer so closely to the Mosaic ordinances of Lev. 9:7 that he takes the writer to have lived after the giving of the Law. John Wesley reads the second clause as "not imputed folly to God": so far was Job from blaspheming that he harboured no dishonourable thought of God, as though he had done anything unworthy of his wisdom, justice, or goodness, but heartily acquiesced in his good pleasure — for discontent and impatience do in effect impute folly to God.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the disputed phrase. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word signifies saltlessness or tastelessness, dealing devoid of sense, and they weigh two renderings — Jerome's "he uttered nothing absurd against God," and the other, "he did not attribute folly to God" — siding, with Hirzel and Schlottmann, for the latter. Charles Ellicott glosses "foolishly" as the word for reproach or guilt, kin to the "unsavoury" of Job 6:6, coming just after Satan's first defeat. Matthew Henry gathers the whole into the Holy Ghost's own testimony to Job's constancy: he did not attribute folly to God, for discontent and impatience charge God with folly, and against their first workings Job carefully watched.

The witnesses do not finally divide, though Keil and Delitzsch drop a sober hint that the verdict covers only "all this" thus far, and that later on Job would commit himself with some unwise thoughts of the government of God. For now, however, the account stands clear: the accuser is answered, the servant is upheld, and the man who has lost everything has neither sinned with his lips nor charged his Maker with folly.
